episodes.title: Fable 5.2 Is the Best AI Ever. So Why Am I Not Switching Yet?
episodes.about: Anthropic's Fable 5.2 is breaking benchmarks and powering ambitious demos, so why isn't it an obvious upgrade for everyday work? NLW examines early reviews and his own experiments to explore where the model outperforms Opus 5.5, where it still falls short, and why its biggest opportunities may require rethinking what we ask AI to do.
episodes.why: Anthropic's Fable 5.2 tops the benchmarks, but NLW's own experiments say switching is not automatic: where it beats Opus 5.5, where it still falls short, and why getting the gain means asking AI for different work.

episodes.title: The US is building the Smartest AI. China is running a different race | Luisa Rodriguez
episodes.about: China's best models are only six months behind America's, despite having far less computing power. Luisa Rodriguez investigates how that is possible: US rules stop Nvidia selling its best chips to China, but Chinese companies can still rent those same chips in data centers abroad, smugglers go to extreme lengths to sneak chips into China, and Chinese AI companies copy America's best models on an industrial scale. The US could tackle these gaps with powers it already has, so the current situation, with China only months behind, is largely a policy choice.
episodes.why: Discovery pick — 80,000 Hours is an interview show about the world's biggest problems, new here: how China stays six months behind US models by renting banned chips abroad and copying models at scale, and why that gap is a policy choice.

episodes.title: Canva Is Tackling AI Design’s Most Frustrating Problem with Stefano Corazza- #784
episodes.about: Stefano Corazza, head of AI research at Canva, explains how his team is building custom models and agents around iterative design workflows. They discuss the tradeoffs between training models from scratch and adapting open-weights models, and how proprietary design data supports specialization. Corazza explains how Craft separates layout planning from pixel generation and how Brush uses design tools and visual feedback to create and revise compositions, plus the challenge of evaluating design quality beyond a single generation, using vision-language models as judges alongside human evaluation.
episodes.why: Canva's AI research head on the design failure everyone hits — the model cannot revise, only re-roll — and the Craft and Brush systems built around layout first, pixels second, and visual feedback.

episodes.title: The Neuron Basis: Goodfire's Curt Tigges on Agentic Interp, Monosemanticity & Reverse Engineering
episodes.about: Goodfire technical staff member Curt Tigges discusses research revealing that individual MLP neurons in modern language models are far more interpretable and functionally bounded than previously thought. Using an automated agent to test hypotheses across architectures like Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Tigges explains how modern gated MLPs act as legible conjunctions and control signals capable of extensive dynamic sparsity without lasting benchmark loss. By showing that many internal representations can be directly enumerated, this work offers an alternative to complex external featurizers and provides practical avenues for behavior monitoring and persona steering.
episodes.why: The long one: an automated agent tested neurons one by one across models like Qwen3.6 and found the insides far more legible than expected, which points to direct ways to monitor and steer behavior.

episodes.title: Reddit pivots to a login-only experience
episodes.about: Reddit announced it will soon require users to log in to see much of the helpful human-generated content on its site. Why? Because traffic, and thus advertising, has taken a hit since AI started summarizing its data. It is the latest development to threaten the old model of the open internet, says Sarah Gilbert, who researches online communities at the Citizens and Technology Lab at Cornell. She says the new login requirement puts up a wall between humans on the internet and is likely to discourage future contributions to the site.
episodes.why: Out today, eight minutes: Reddit is putting its posts behind a login because AI summaries took the traffic and the ad money with it — one concrete break in the open web's model.
